notes:
I have gathered extensive material from the permitted sources. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes. I was unable to fetch some additional tradition-specific pages due to tool limits, but the sources obtained (Enduring Word, Gill, Ellicott, JFB, Precept Austin, and Clarke) represent Baptist, Anglican, Reformed/Presbyterian, Pentecostal, Methodist, and broad Evangelical traditions respectively.

---

## JUDGES 3 — VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### Overview of the Chapter

Commentators across traditions agree that Judges 3 introduces the "cycle" pattern that governs the entire book: sin → servitude → supplication → salvation → rest. Ellicott calls the section beginning at v. 5 "a history of sin repeating itself, and of Divine Grace constantly devising new remedies" (citing Prof. Cassel). Precept Austin charts the repeating cycle as: Rest → Rebellion → Retribution → Repentance → Restoration.

---

### v. 1: *"These are the nations that the LORD left to test all the Israelites who had not known any of the wars in Canaan..."*

- **God's sovereign purpose.** The nations were left by God deliberately. JFB notes this "evinces the direct influence of the theocracy under which the Israelites were placed." These nations served a double purpose: moral/spiritual discipline and military training (JFB).  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm

- **"To test" (Hebrew *nacah*).** Precept Austin provides an extensive word study, noting that *nacah* means "to prove by trial" — showing what someone is really like through difficulty. It is the same verb used of God testing Abraham (Gen 22:1). The Septuagint translates it *peirazo*, a morally neutral word; the intent of the tester determines whether it is for good or evil. God does not tempt to evil (James 1:13).  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_3_commentary

- **A generation that "had not known."** Gill explains this refers to those not born, or too young to bear arms during Joshua's conquest. Ellicott says it "clearly implies the generation after that of Joshua." The implication is they had no firsthand experience of God's mighty acts in war.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

- **Enduring Word** (David Guzik, Pentecostal/Charismatic tradition): God allowed the nations to remain because Israel had failed to drive them out — "a combination of both their choice and God's will." God doesn't instantly change every area of a believer's life; He leaves challenges so faith can be "proved and improved."  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

---

### v. 2: *"...if only to teach warfare to the subsequent generations of Israel, especially to those who had not known it formerly..."*

- **Learning war.** JFB says God wanted the young "to learn the use of weapons and the art of wielding them." Ellicott adds the lesson was that "they could only learn successfully by the help of God." Gill suggests an alternative interpretation — that God left the nations so Israel would know "what war was, and the sad effects of it; and the difference of fighting with their enemies alone… and the Lord fighting along with them."  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html

- **Spiritual warfare application.** Precept Austin (citing Gary Inrig) says: "The Lord uses those difficulties to teach us how to wage spiritual war… We cannot stand still in our Christian experience. There are enemies to be faced." Guzik (Enduring Word) adds: "The symbol of Christianity is a cross, not a feather bed."  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_3_commentary  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

---

### v. 3: *"...the five rulers of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites who lived in the mountains of Lebanon from Mount Baal-hermon to Lebo-hamath."*

- **The specific enemies.** Gill identifies the five Philistine lords as rulers of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron. The Sidonians were the inhabitants of the famous city Sidon, named after Canaan's firstborn (Gen 10:15). The Hivites lived in Mount Lebanon in the north. "From Mount Baal-hermon to the entering in of Hamath" marks the northern boundary of Canaan.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html

- **"Lords" (Hebrew *Seranim*).** Ellicott notes this is a technical title for Philistine rulers — rendered "satrapies" by the LXX and "satraps" by the Vulgate. Baal-hermon is probably another name for Baal-gad, likely Paneas/Caesarea Philippi.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

- **Guzik** points out that God "named each of the pagan peoples." In the same way, believers can identify their specific spiritual enemies by name.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

---

### v. 4: *"These nations were left to test the Israelites, to find out whether they would keep the commandments of the LORD, which He had given their fathers through Moses."*

- **Testing obedience to God's word.** Gill explains the test was to "prove their faithfulness to God" — specifically "all the commandments… moral, civil, and ceremonial, and particularly those that concerned the destruction of the Canaanites, their altars, and their idols" (Deut 7:1). Precept Austin notes the purpose was "to determine if Israel was truly loyal" and to "reveal otherwise hidden character qualities."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_3_commentary

- **Warren Wiersbe** (cited by Precept Austin): "When God puts His own people into the furnace, He keeps His eye on the clock and His hand on the thermostat. He knows how long and how much."  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_3_commentary

---

### v. 5: *"Thus the Israelites continued to live among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites."*

- **The compromise of co-existence.** Gill notes the irony: they "dwelt among the Canaanites, as if they had been only sojourners with them, and not conquerors of them; and dwelt by sufferance, and not as proprietors." JFB says "the two peoples by degrees came to be on habits of intercourse." Ellicott observes this verse begins the "second great section" of the book. This is the list of nations from Exod 33:2; the Girgashites are added in Josh 24:11.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

---

### v. 6: *"And they took the daughters of these people in marriage, gave their own daughters to their sons, and served their gods."*

- **Intermarriage as the gateway to idolatry.** Gill calls this a direct violation of the "express command of God" in Deut 7:3, noting the result was they "confounded their families, debased their blood, and were ensnared into idolatry." Ellicott says the intermarriages show "we are now a generation removed from the days of Joshua." JFB similarly says "reciprocal alliances were formed by marriage till the Israelites, relaxing the austerity of their principles, showed a growing conformity to the manners and worship of their idolatrous neighbors."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm

- **Guzik** (Enduring Word) applies this pastorally: "Jesus told us that following Him would require that we give up the things we love most (Mark 10:29-30). Often an ungodly romantic relationship falls into this exact category."  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

---

### v. 7: *"So the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD; they forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asherahs."*

- **"Forgot the LORD."** Gill says it was "as if they had never heard of him, or known him, their Maker and Preserver, who had done so many great and good things for them."

- **Baals and Asherahs.** Ellicott provides a detailed note: "Asherah" (plural Asheroth/Asherim) refers to "wooden images of the nature-goddess Asherah." He clarifies the old KJV rendering "groves" is mistaken — the Vulgate rendered it "Astaroth," but Mövers' research shows Asherah and Astarte were "different though allied deities." The word comes from a root meaning "upright." Gill notes that Baalim were originally "deified kings and heroes" and that groves were commonly associated with idol temples.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html

---

### v. 8: *"Then the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram-naharaim, and the Israelites served him eight years."*

- **"He sold them."** JFB explains this means God "delivered them" into the enemy's hand — not a literal sale but the language of covenantal abandonment.

- **The name "Cushan-rishathaim."** Ellicott calls it "a term of hatred rather than a name" — it means "Cushan of the double wickedness." Gill agrees: "Rishathaim" means "two wickednesses." Guzik (citing Cundall) says the name "reads literally 'Cushan of double wickedness', not likely a personal name, and it would appear that the historian has made a deliberate distortion to cast ridicule upon this oppressor." The Targum calls him "Cushan, the wicked king of Syria."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

- **Aram-naharaim = Mesopotamia.** Literally "Syria of the two rivers" (Tigris and Euphrates). This first oppressor came from the distant north-east.  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm

- **Reformed/Presbyterian perspective (JFB):** The servitude was "by the payment of a stipulated tribute yearly, the raising of which must have caused a great amount of labor and privation."  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm

---

### v. 9: *"But when the Israelites cried out to the LORD, He raised up Othniel son of Caleb's younger brother Kenaz as a deliverer to save them."*

- **"Cried out to the LORD."** Ellicott connects this to the pattern of Neh 9:27 and Ps 107:13 — "In their distress they had recourse to earnest prayer, accompanied by humble and penitent confession." JFB says the same.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

- **Othniel.** Gill notes he was the same Othniel who took Debir and married Achsah, Caleb's daughter (Judges 1:12-13). Clarke (Methodist/Wesleyan tradition) calls him "this noble Hebrew" who was "of the tribe of Judah, and nephew and son-in-law to Caleb, whose praise stands without abatement in the sacred records."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/judges-3.html

- **The word "deliverer" (Hebrew *moshia*).** Ellicott notes the LXX renders it "a saviour" (comp. Luke 1:69; Acts 13:23). The same word is used in Neh 9:27 for the judges collectively.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

---

### v. 10: *"The Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and he became Israel's judge and went out to war. And the LORD delivered Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram into the hand of Othniel, who prevailed against him."*

- **"The Spirit of the LORD came upon him."** This is the key to Othniel's success. Clarke says "by his natural valour, experience in war, and the peculiar influence of the Divine Spirit, he was well qualified." The Targum interprets this as "the spirit of prophecy." JFB says he was "impelled by a supernatural influence" — first pursuing moral reformation, abolition of idolatry, and revival of pure religion, then gathering warriors. Gill similarly says the Spirit "moved him to engage in this work… inspired him with courage, and filled him with every needful gift."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/judges-3.html  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html

- **"He judged Israel."** Ellicott notes some Rabbis explain "judged" (*yishpot*) here to mean "avenged" (as in Ps 43:1), "possibly from disliking the notion of a Kenizzite… holding the office of a judge." But the text plainly states he functioned as judge. Ellicott also notes the Jewish tradition that places Othniel highest among the judges — applying to him Song 4:7 ("Thou art all fair; there is no spot in thee") because he is the only judge "represented as irreproachable."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

- **Guzik** (Pentecostal/Charismatic perspective): Othniel "lived the principle of Zechariah 4:6: 'Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of hosts.' Empowered by the Spirit of the LORD, he delivered Israel." He adds (citing Cundall): "Since Pentecost (Acts 2) a more general and permanent endowment of the Holy Spirit has been the privilege of every disciple."  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

- **Clarke** (Methodist): adds that Othniel's receiving the Spirit "shows that the political state of the Jews was still a theocracy. No man attempted to do any thing in that state without the immediate inspiration of God."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/judges-3.html

---

### v. 11: *"So the land had rest for forty years, until Othniel son of Kenaz died."*

- **Forty years of rest.** Ellicott raises chronological difficulties: "No less than fifty schemes of the chronology of the period of the judges have been attempted, which fact alone proves how insufficient are the data." He questions whether the forty years include or exclude the servitude, and whether the periods of rest and servitude are continuous or overlapping in different regions. He also notes Othniel's possible extreme age — if he was forty at his marriage and Joshua lived to 110, Othniel would have been about 143 at death.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

- **JFB** quotes Bishop Hall: "How powerful the influence of one good man is, in church or state, is best found in his loss."  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm

- **Gill** notes that some Jewish commentators (Ben Gersom, Abarbinel) include the eight years' servitude within the forty years of rest.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html

---

### v. 12: *"Once again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD. So He gave Eglon king of Moab power over Israel, because they had done evil in the sight of the LORD."*

- **The cycle repeats.** JFB: "The Israelites, deprived of the moral and political influences of Othniel, were not long in following their native bias to idolatry." Ellicott says "did evil again" is literally "added to do evil" (*wayyosipu*), a Hebraism found even in the NT (Luke 20:11-12).  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

- **"The LORD strengthened Eglon."** Gill: God "put it into his heart to invade them, and encouraged him to it, and gave him success." The Jewish tradition holds that Ruth was the daughter of Eglon (Ruth 1:4). Ellicott notes the name Eglon means "a fat bullock" (cf. Ps 22:12; Amos 4:1) — possibly another contemptuous name given by the biblical writer.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

- **Reformed view (JFB):** Eglon's ambition was "to recover that extensive portion of his ancient territory possessed by the Israelites." He is the successor of Balak.  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm

---

### v. 13: *"After enlisting the Ammonites and Amalekites to join forces with him, Eglon attacked and defeated Israel, taking possession of the City of Palms."*

- **The coalition.** Ellicott notes Ammon and Moab were closely allied by race and character (Gen 19:37-38). The Amalekites were "the wild desert clans" who had been Israel's "bitterest enemies" since the wilderness. Guzik (citing Cundall) describes Ammon as "to the north-east of Moab" and Amalek as "a nomadic race occupying the considerable area south of Judah, and were possibly Israel's bitterest enemy."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

- **"City of Palms" = Jericho.** All sources agree. JFB (citing Josephus) says Eglon "erected fortifications in the territory adjoining Jericho" and fixed his residence there. Gill notes the city itself was destroyed by Joshua and not rebuilt until Ahab's time, so Eglon possessed the surrounding area, possibly building "a fort or garrison here, to secure the fords of Jordan."  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html

---

### v. 14: *"The Israelites served Eglon king of Moab eighteen years."*

- **Eighteen years.** Gill notes this was "ten years longer than they served the king of Mesopotamia… as a severer correction of them for their relapse into idolatry." Guzik says "Sin always brings bondage, though it comes deceptively. The fish never contemplates the bondage of the hook when it goes after the bait; Satan snares people by making the bait attractive and hiding the hook."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

---

### v. 15: *"And again they cried out to the LORD, and He raised up Ehud son of Gera, a left-handed Benjamite, as their deliverer. So they sent him with tribute to Eglon king of Moab."*

- **"Left-handed" (Hebrew *itter yad-yemino*).** Literally "restricted/shut as to his right hand." Ellicott argues this cannot mean "ambidextrous" as the LXX and Vulgate translate — the Hebrew *itter* means "shut" (cf. Ps 69:16, "lest the pit shut her mouth"). He suggests Ehud may have had an accident that maimed his right hand, like a Hebrew Scaevola. JFB notes the Benjamite tribe was known for left-handed warriors (Judges 20:16) but acknowledges some versions render the word "both-handed." Guzik (citing Cundall) says "in the eyes of an Israelite, this was regarded as a physical defect."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

- **The tribute.** Gill says the "present" (Hebrew *minchah*) was either the yearly tribute or a gift to reconcile them to Eglon. Ellicott notes *minchah* is used "euphemistically for 'tribute'" elsewhere (2 Sam 8:6; 1 Kgs 4:21; Ps 72:10).  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

- **Clarke** (Methodist): "Presents, tribute, etc., in the eastern countries were offered with very great ceremony; and to make the more parade several persons, ordinarily slaves, sumptuously dressed, and in considerable number, were employed to carry what would not be a burden even to one."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/judges-3.html

---

### v. 16: *"Now Ehud had made for himself a double-edged sword a cubit long. He strapped it to his right thigh under his cloak..."*

- **The dagger.** JFB says the measurement "a cubit" uses the rare Hebrew word *gomed* (not the usual *ammah*). Ellicott notes the LXX and Vulgate render it "a span long" (*spithames*, *palmae*), but "a dagger of a span long hardly… suits the following narrative, and perhaps *gomed* is an archaic word for *ammah*." It originally meant "a staff."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

- **Right thigh.** JFB: "The sword was usually worn on the left side; so that Ehud's was the more likely to escape detection." Ellicott adds: "Doubtless the war-cloak was flung in folds over the left shoulder, and Eglon, unaware that the bearer of the tribute was left-handed, would see that the side at which arms were usually worn was covered with a flowing robe, and would not suspect the dagger hidden at the right side."  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

---

### v. 17: *"...and brought the tribute to Eglon king of Moab, who was an obese man."*

- **Eglon's obesity.** Ellicott says the Vulgate calls him *Crassus nimis*. The notice is "inserted with reference to v. 22." The LXX renders the word as *asteios* — which may mean either "graceful" or more probably here, "ridiculous." Guzik (citing Clarke): "The word Eglon signifies a little calf! … In Eglon's case, it was a fatted calf and was ready for slaughter."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

---

### v. 18: *"After Ehud had finished presenting the tribute, he ushered out those who had carried it."*

- **Strategic dismissal.** Ellicott: "The plan of Ehud was deeply laid. He wished (1) to secure his end, which would be more difficult amid the soldiers and attendants… (2) to avoid endangering his comrades; (3) to provide, if possible, for his own escape. By going away with the deputation… he would still more lull suspicion asleep."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

- **The tribute-bearers.** Ellicott notes that "according to the fashion of the East," the tribute would be carried "in long and pompous array" — "fifty persons often bear what one man could easily carry" (Chardin).  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

---

### v. 19: *"But upon reaching the idols near Gilgal, he himself turned back and said, 'I have a secret message for you, O king.' 'Silence,' said the king, and all his attendants left him."*

- **"Idols" (Hebrew *pesilim*).** JFB renders this "graven images" — "statues of Moabite idols, the sight of which kindled the patriotic zeal of Ehud to avenge this public insult to Israel on its author." Ellicott agrees: it means "idols of some kind — probably those of Moab." Some explain them as the twelve stones from the Jordan set up at Gilgal (Josh 4:2). The KJV renders "quarries," following the Chaldee and Rabbi Jarchi.  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

- **"A secret message" / "Keep silence."** Ellicott: the Hebrew is *Has* — "Hush!" — a graphic touch. It is unclear whether the king said "Hush!" to Ehud (to prevent him speaking before the attendants left) or to the attendants as a signal to withdraw. Either way, "they at once understood that the king wished to be left alone."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

---

### v. 20: *"Then Ehud approached him while he was sitting alone in the coolness of his upper room. 'I have a word from God for you,' Ehud said, and the king rose from his seat."*

- **"Summer parlour" / "upper room of cooling."** Ellicott describes it as the *alijah* (Greek *hyperoon*, Mark 14:15) — the coolest part of an Eastern house. The detail "reminds us that the scene… is placed in the Ghôr — the Jordan valley, which lies nearly a thousand feet below the level of the Mediterranean, and is probably the hottest district in the world."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

- **"A message from God."** Ellicott says: "The whole narrative implies that Ehud was, to some extent, an honoured person even among the Moabites. Probably he was reckoned as a prophet. In the East sacred claims are readily conceded, even to enemies." The king rose "probably out of reverence, to receive the Divine message." Gill says "it was the Lord that spoke to him by an impulse on his spirit, and the thing was from the Lord he was to do, for nothing less could have justified him in such an action."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html

- **Spurgeon** (cited by Enduring Word / Guzik): "Ehud said, 'I have a message from God for thee.' It was a dagger which found its way to Eglon's heart, and he fell dead. So shall death deliver his message to you." Spurgeon also applies this to preaching: "I am afraid, there are some ministers who hardly think that the gospel is intended to come personally home to the people."  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

- **F.B. Meyer** (cited by Guzik): "God's Word pierces as a two-edged sword to the dividing of soul and spirit in the recesses of the being, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart. When the Eglon of self has received its death-wound, the glad trumpet of freedom is blown on the hills."  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

---

### vv. 21–22: *"And Ehud reached with his left hand, pulled the sword from his right thigh, and plunged it into Eglon's belly. Even the handle sank in after the blade, and Eglon's fat closed in over it, so that Ehud did not withdraw the sword from his belly. And Eglon's bowels emptied."*

- **The graphic details.** JFB: "The whole circumstance of this daring act — the death of Eglon without a shriek, or noise — the locking of the doors — the carrying off the key — the calm, unhurried deportment of Ehud — show the strength of his confidence that he was doing God service."  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm

- **"Bowels emptied" / translation difficulties.** Guzik (citing Clarke, Cundall, and Wolf) explains several interpretations: (a) the contents of the bowels issued through the wound; (b) Eglon had an evacuation through fright; (c) the most plausible is "the downward motion of the dagger being with such force that it passed completely through the abdomen and projected from the vent" (so the RV: "it came out behind"). The KJV and RSV translate "and the dirt came out." One word in this phrase "occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament" (Cundall).  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

- **Moral question of assassination.** Ellicott says clearly: "the act by which he achieved his end was unjustifiable. To quote his example in defence of the principle of assassination is a gross abuse of Scripture." He notes that "those who defend the murder do so by assuming that the Divine call to Ehud to deliver his people sanctioned and possibly even suggested the means by which it was accomplished. But such methods of inferential exegesis undermine the very bases of morals."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html

- **Guzik** notes Wolf's observation: "God did not necessarily approve of the method used by Ehud. It may be significant that the Spirit of the Lord did not come on Ehud and that he was never described as 'judging Israel.'" Nevertheless, "the Bible reliably records this incident without giving specific approval of this act of assassination."  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

---

### vv. 23–25: *"Then Ehud went out through the porch, closing and locking the doors of the upper room behind him. After Ehud was gone, Eglon's servants came in and found the doors of the upper room locked. 'He must be relieving himself in the cool room,' they said. So they waited until they became worried..."*

- **The servants' assumption.** Guzik explains that "attending to his needs" is literally "covering his feet" — "a euphemism for elimination also used in 1 Samuel 24:3." Clarke notes that some commentators see this only reluctantly and prefer to think the king was sleeping: "He has lain down on his sofa in order to sleep; when this was done they dropped their slippers, lifted up their feet, and covered them with their long loose garments." But Clarke says "the versions, in general seem to understand it as implying a certain natural act."

- **The trumpet call.** JFB says he "summoned to arms the people of that mountainous region, which, adjoining the territory of Benjamin, had probably suffered most from the grievous oppression of the Moabites."

### v. 31: *"After Ehud came Shamgar son of Anath. And he too saved Israel, striking down six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad."*

- **"Shamgar."** JFB notes: "No notice is given of the tribe or family of this judge; and from the Philistines being the enemy that roused him into public service, the suffering seems to have been local — confined to some of the western tribes." Gill says "who he was, and who his father, and of what tribe, we nowhere else read." Bochart conjectured Shamgar and Lycurgus may be the same figure.  
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html

- **The oxgoad.** JFB describes it as "eight feet long and about six inches in circumference. Such an instrument, wielded by a strong arm, would do no mean execution." They add: "We may suppose… that Shamgar was only the leader of a band of peasants, who by means of such implements of labor as they could lay hold of at the moment, achieved the heroic exploit recorded."

- **Guzik** (Enduring Word): "Shamgar is an excellent example of service for God. He simply used what God put in his hand — in his case, an ox goad… God uses whatever simple tools are in our hands when we're willing to act for Him."

## TRADITION-SPECIFIC DIFFERENCES

The sources retrieved show more convergence than divergence on Judges 3. However, several distinct emphases emerge:

**1. On the Morality of Ehud's Assassination (vv. 20–22)**

- **Anglican/Ellicott:** Strongly condemns the act as "unjustifiable" and warns that defending it by inferring divine sanction "undermine[s] the very bases of morals." He connects it historically with the papal approval of the assassinations of Henry IV.
- **Reformed/JFB:** More measured — says the whole episode shows Ehud's "confidence that he was doing God service," without explicit moral condemnation.
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** Acknowledges the moral difficulty but notes the Spirit is never said to come upon Ehud and he is never called a "judge" — yet also notes that Ehud truthfully said "I have a message from God."
- **Baptist/Gill:** States that God spoke to Ehud "by an impulse on his spirit" and "nothing less could have justified him in such an action" — implying divine warrant.
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/judges-3.html

**2. The Meaning of "Left-Handed" (v. 15)**

- **Anglican/Ellicott:** Argues *itter* means "shut" (maimed), not ambidextrous — Ehud may have had a disabled right hand, making him like a Hebrew Scaevola.
- **JFB:** Acknowledges "some versions" render it "both-handed" (citing 1 Chr 12:2), but the peculiarity "distinguished many in the Benjamite tribe."
- **Guzik/Cundall:** Emphasises it was "regarded as a physical defect" in ancient Israel, making Ehud an unlikely hero whom God used.
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/judges-3.html
  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_003.cfm
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

**3. The Holy Spirit's Work (v. 10)**

- **Methodist/Clarke:** Emphasises the theocratic dimension — the Spirit's coming upon Othniel "shows that the political state of the Jews was still a theocracy." This reflects the Wesleyan emphasis on God's direct government.
- **Pentecostal/Guzik:** Connects this OT empowering to the NT — "Since Pentecost (Acts 2) a more general and permanent endowment of the Holy Spirit has been the privilege of every disciple." This reflects the Charismatic emphasis on the Spirit's empowerment for all believers.
- **Reformed/Gill:** The Targum interprets it as "the spirit of prophecy," but Gill himself thinks "it seems rather to be the spirit of counsel and courage, of strength and fortitude of body and mind."
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/judges-3.html
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-3/

## OTHER VIEWS

I was unable to retrieve specific pages from **Catholic, Orthodox, modern scholarship** (NET Bible, Bible Odyssey), or **Lutheran** sources due to tool limits. However, from the sources obtained, these points are relevant:

- **Catholic connections (via Ellicott):** Ellicott references St. Francis of Assisi being received with respect by Muslims (on the idea that sacred claims are conceded even to enemies), and mentions Pope Paul V's reaction to the murder of Henry IV — both Catholic historical references.
- **Jewish tradition (via Gill and Ellicott):** The Rabbis placed Othniel highest among the judges and identified him with Jabez (1 Chr 4:10). They said Shamgar judged only one year. Cushan-rishathaim's "two wickednesses" were said to refer to Balaam and Cushan.
- **Chronological debates (via Ellicott):** "No less than fifty schemes of the chronology of the period of the judges have been attempted, which fact alone proves how insufficient are the data on which to decide." This reflects ongoing scholarly uncertainty about whether the periods of rest and servitude are consecutive or overlapping.
